title: Two takes on Illustrative Math
author: John Seelke
summary: John Seelke, a mathematics teacher with more than 25 years of experience, responds to the recent criticism of the Illustrative Math curriculum that followed Sold a Story 2. He first concedes two real weaknesses, namely too few practice problems and a technology-driven design that lacks clear worked examples for a parent or student to consult. He then defends two overlooked strengths. By his count the curriculum spends four lessons building decimal multiplication from powers of ten, fractions and area models, where one older textbook he owns covers the same ground in less than one, and its geometry course teaches triangle congruence through rigid transformations rather than memorised postulates. He argues that teachers' complaints usually reflect their own unfamiliarity with these methods, a problem of teacher understanding that the critics rarely address. His closing claim is that different does not mean bad, because students vary and some will only grasp an idea when it is shown several ways, a lesson he took from his own early habit of teaching exactly as he had been taught.
points: Seelke concedes the strongest criticisms, thin practice sets and a lack of clear worked examples, which gives his defence of the curriculum more credibility than a blanket endorsement would.

Counting lessons rather than pages, he shows Illustrative Math building decimal multiplication slowly from powers of ten, fractions and area models, so the apparent slowness is a deliberate sequencing choice.

He locates much of the resistance in teacher understanding rather than curriculum flaws, noting that coached teachers disliked it because it differed from how they were taught and they did not fully follow the lessons.

He pushes back on explicit-instruction advocates by asking why all students should be taught the same thing the same way, and presents multiple representations as eye opening for some students and redundant for others.
He raises an honest question about the lack of formal proofs, which he sees as a foundational reasoning skill nearly erased from curricula.
quotes: That is a big concern about Illustrative Math, one that I agree with. Another concern that I have is that the Illustrative Math curriculum, as it’s written these days, is both technology driven and lacks clear examples of problems.

Those against Illustrative Math discuss how students have to discover ideas on their own and there is often they are lost. Some see this as going too fast. And yet, IM does over four lessons what at least one textbook does in less than one (considering that it combines addition and subtraction with multiplication).

I’m a math major who has taught math for over 25 years and at first glance I had to pause and consider what some of the questions were asking. For many teachers, this would be a turn off for a curriculum - how can I teach something if I don’t understand it.

They also didn’t understand why one needed to take four days to teach a topic that was normally taught in one day. This does not necessarily mean that the curriculum is flawed, but rather points to a deeper problem that is not addressed in Sold a Story 2 and is rarely discussed - teacher understanding.
Different does not mean bad. Different means another perspective or another point of view. Many think of mathematics as a course where there is one right answer and there is one way to do things.
If we acknowledge that not every student is exactly the same, then why do advocates of explicit instruction believe that all students should be taught the same thing, the same way?
Now I provide students multiple ways to see the math. For some, they may think it’s redundant. But for others, its eye opening.
